title: Rival theaters and their French and American audiences
summary: The Camp Street and St. Charles theaters competed with the French Orleans Theater for audiences.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: What about the audience now? It wouldn't be all French, certainly.

No, it was, again, amusements were limited. However, after the American Theater opened, even the one on Camp Street and then later the St. Charles, there was a great tendency for the French to go to their side and the Americans to go to their side. But both theaters, this is true more often than the American Theater, tried to bring in attractions that would draw the patrons away from the other theater. Thus the American Theater would bring in French dancers, Celestine and Constance and things like that, hoping to draw the audience away from the French theater. But this only led to a great many Frenchmen to complain that they were denied the pleasure of seeing these dancers, since they didn't appear in the French theater. They considered they were denied the possibility and they would importune the management to get them over to their side so that they could go with propriety and see them. A good deal of rivalry that way. But always there were a great many English-speaking Americans or English-stock Americans who would contend French theater and vice versa.
